text.p: British broker Willis Corroon on Friday announced it was liquidating its Sovereign Marine Insurance subsidiary following an arbitration award which could cost it tens of millions of pounds.
The arbitration decision, which involved one of Sovereign's reinsurers, will not have any financial impact on Willis itself with any potential losses ultimately being borne by Sovereign clients.
According to Willis, the effect of the arbitration decision could have implications for other reinsurance contracts.
The award substantially increased Sovereign's liabilities and would have required the provision of additional capital from Willis to avoid liquidation.
At the end of 1996, Sovereign's reinsurance recoveries were valued at 168 million pounds ($283.4 million).

The arbitration decision, however, calls this figure into question and the eventual hit could be anywhere between the 10.2 million pounds of the disputed reinsurance contract and the 168 million pounds of possible reinsurance recoveries.
Willis chairman John Reeve said the decision to wind up Sovereign had been taken with regret but that it was in the best interests of shareholders.

"We have already committed substantial group resources to maintaining Sovereign's solvency since the company went into run-off in 1991. The board cannot justify a continuation of this commitment," said Reeve.
Willis shares fell on the news, finishing the day seven pence lower at 136-1/2 pence.

Losses at Sovereign had cost the group over 72 million pounds since it was put into run-off in 1991. The decision to put it into liquidation will bring to an end the risk of the need for further provisions.
While analysts accepted there was unlikely to be a direct financial impact from the liquidation, they expressed concern about the effect on the group's broker relationships.
"Unlike a stand alone insurance company, this insurance underwritng operation is owned by a broker, which has relationships across the world," said Credit Lyonnais insurance analyst Robin Savage.
"The question is: Can it actually stand by and let its underwriting operation go into insolvent liquidation and not make the payments? If it does, what is that going to do to is broking business?"
But Willis' director of corporate communications Peter Stevens said the company believed it would not affect Willis's ongoing business.

"Professionals in the insurance market understand the business they are in. They understand that Sovereign is only the latest in a long line of companies that has been unable to keep up the pace of the 1980s and will understand that we didn't have any option," said Stevens.
In a separate move, Willis also said it had agreed in principle to purchase a one-third stake in the largest independent French insurance broker, Gras Savoye & Cie.
Investment by the group in Gras Savoye and the consequent pooling of capabilities would create a powerful combination in the French market-place, said Reeve.
Like Willis, Gras Savoye has come under increasing pressure following a series of mergers in the industry which have left them trailing far behind American rivals Marsh & Mclennan and Aon.
Gras Savoye was a member of Unison, an international network of independent insurance brokers which effectively ceased to exist when U.S. broker Johnson & Higgins was acquired by March & Mclennan.
The Willis transaction is dependent on the satisfactory completion of the group's due diligence procedures and the approval of the shareholders.
Willis also announced it had acquired all the outstanding shares in its Brazilian associate York Willis Corroon Corretores de Seguros SA in which it has held a 30 percent stake in York since 1990.
($ = 0.592 British Pounds)
